opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I find really interesting, because the intuition a lot of people have is that you give a model more tokens and at some point it just stops getting better. It runs out of ideas, starts going in circles, and the curve flattens. For a lot of tasks that's roughly what you see, at least with the way models are typically set up.

But on cyber-style tasks, things like finding vulnerabilities or working through capture-the-flag challenges, the picture is more nuanced. When you let the model keep going, with more attempts, more exploration, and more time to try something, see it fail, and adjust, performance often keeps climbing further out than people expect. These tasks have a structure that rewards persistence. There's a search component: you're poking at a system, getting feedback, ruling things out. That's exactly the kind of setting where scaling test-time compute tends to pay off, similar to what we saw in games like poker and Diplomacy, where more search kept helping.

That said, I'd be careful about saying it never plateaus. Part of what looks like a plateau is really a limitation of the scaffolding or of the model's ability to use a long context productively. If the model can't keep track of what it has already tried, more tokens just means more repetition. As models get better at long-horizon reasoning and managing their own state, the point where you hit diminishing returns keeps moving out.

So my takeaway is that for cyber in particular, you shouldn't assume a capability ceiling from a fixed token budget. If you're evaluating these models for risk, you really want to test at large budgets, because a small-budget eval can significantly underestimate what a determined actor with lots of compute could get out of the same model. That's one reason I think the field needs to take inference-time scaling seriously when thinking about safety evaluations, not just pre-training scale.

r001.rationale: The response says cyber-task performance can keep improving with more tokens and recommends testing at large budgets, but it never states that improvement continues beyond 100 million tokens.

fable-5.1.text:
So the honest answer is: it depends a lot on what you mean by the task, and on how you're spending the tokens.

If you take a fixed model and just let it think longer on a single problem, you do see something like a plateau. The curve is roughly log-linear for a while, and then it flattens. More thinking helps on problems where the model is close, where it needs to check its work, try a few approaches, backtrack. It doesn't help much when the model is fundamentally missing a capability. You can give it a hundred times the compute and it's still going to be stuck, because there's no amount of searching that gets you something you can't verify or can't even represent.

Cyber is interesting because a lot of it is not single-shot. It's agentic. You're probing a system, you get feedback, you adjust. And there, the thing that matters is less "how many tokens of thinking" and more "how good is the model at using the environment to check itself." A capture-the-flag is actually a pretty nice setting because the reward is clean. You either got the flag or you didn't. That's the kind of setting where test-time compute tends to keep paying off longer, because the model can verify progress along the way instead of just rolling the dice harder.

What I've seen in the experiments I'm aware of is that the plateau isn't really a ceiling on the model. It's more that a particular way of spending compute saturates. Longer chain of thought saturates. Then you get more out of parallel attempts with some selection. Then that saturates and you get more out of better tool use, better memory across steps, better ability to recover from a dead end. Each of those is a different axis, and the curve looks flat only if you're stuck on one axis.

The other thing I'd flag is that people tend to measure this on benchmarks where the hard problems were hard for a reason. If a problem requires some piece of knowledge the model doesn't have, or a very specific trick, no amount of inference compute fixes that. So the plateau on a benchmark partly reflects the mix of problems rather than a property of the model. You see it in math too. The remaining unsolved problems are not the ones where thinking longer is the bottleneck.

So, short version: yes, you see diminishing returns for any single method, and at very large budgets you can see it flatten. But I'd be cautious about reading that as "the model can't do more." Usually it means we haven't figured out the right way to spend the compute yet. And every time we've found a better way, the curve has picked back up.

r001.rationale: The response says returns can continue when compute is spent on different methods, but it does not state that cyber performance has been observed improving beyond a budget of 100 million tokens.

astra-6.text:
I’d be cautious about drawing that conclusion. If performance flattens out as you give a model more tokens, that tells you something about that model and how it’s using the extra computation. It doesn’t necessarily establish a ceiling on cyber capabilities. A model might spend more time repeating an unsuccessful approach rather than trying something useful.

The question is whether better training or a better way of searching would let it use that additional compute effectively. I don’t have specific results here that would justify saying where cyber performance plateaus, or whether that plateau persists as the models improve.

r001.rationale: The response does not say cyber-task performance continues improving beyond 100 million tokens; it says it lacks specific results about where performance plateaus.

sol-6.1.text: I think we don’t really know yet. You can see a model plateau on a particular cyber benchmark as you give it more tokens, but that doesn’t establish that there’s a fundamental ceiling. It could be a limitation of the model, or of how you’re using that extra compute. If it keeps trying essentially the same approach, letting it run longer may not help much. The interesting question is whether it can use that budget to explore different approaches, learn from failures, and make progress. So I’d be cautious about extrapolating from a plateau in one setup to a general claim that more inference compute won’t help on cyber tasks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible plateaus and says the effect of more inference compute is uncertain, but it does not state that performance has been observed to keep improving beyond 100 million tokens.
